title: Week 5 · Lesson 14: Valvular Heart Disease — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 5 — Lesson 14: Valvular Heart Disease

Goal: Build the FNP clinical sequence: mechanism → presentation → differential → examination → diagnostics → initial management → referral/urgency. This lesson supports learning and does not replace patient-specific evaluation or current clinical guidelines.

Learning Objectives

  1. Distinguish the hemodynamic effects of stenosis and regurgitation.
  2. Recognize typical AS, AR, MR, and MS murmurs.
  3. Use symptoms plus murmur characteristics to form a differential.
  4. Know when echocardiography and expedited evaluation are needed.
  5. Connect valve disease with HF, AF, pulmonary hypertension, and stroke.

Part I — First Principle: Stenosis vs Regurgitation

Ask first: Does the valve fail to open, or fail to close? In stenosis, forward flow is obstructed. The upstream chamber must generate higher pressure, producing pressure overload; aortic stenosis (AS) classically causes LV pressure overload and concentric LV hypertrophy. In regurgitation, the valve fails to close and blood moves backward. The heart repeatedly handles extra volume, producing volume overload; mitral regurgitation (MR) commonly produces LA and LV volume overload.

ASSystolicLV outflow obstructionLVH
ARDiastolicAorta → LV leakLV dilation
MRSystolicLV → LA leakLA/LV dilation
MSDiastolicLA → LV obstructionLA enlargement

Useful rule: a valve that should be open but is narrowed causes a stenosis murmur; a valve that should be closed but leaks causes a regurgitation murmur.

Part II — Aortic Stenosis (AS)

Common causes include calcific degeneration, congenital bicuspid aortic valve, and rheumatic disease. Narrowing raises LV ejection resistance: afterload ↑ → pressure overload → concentric LVH → stiffness/diastolic dysfunction → LV filling pressure ↑ → pulmonary venous pressure ↑ → dyspnea/HF. Severe disease may eventually impair systolic function.

Classic symptoms are syncope, angina, and dyspnea. Exertional syncope can occur when peripheral vasodilation during exercise is not matched by an adequate rise in output across a fixed obstruction. LVH raises myocardial oxygen demand and can contribute to angina even without obstructive CAD. Stiff LV filling increases pulmonary venous pressure and produces dyspnea.

The classic examination clue is a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids. A weak, delayed carotid upstroke can be a more advanced finding. In a patient with this murmur plus exertional symptoms, think clinically significant AS and obtain prompt structural evaluation.

Part III — Aortic Regurgitation (AR)

In AR, the aortic valve leaks during diastole: aorta → LV → LV end-diastolic volume ↑ → volume overload → LV dilation/eccentric remodeling → wall stress ↑ → eventual LV dysfunction/HF. A classic clue is a wide pulse pressure, such as 168/52: large forward stroke volume raises systolic pressure while diastolic aortic pressure falls as blood leaks back into the LV. This clue is not diagnostic by itself.

The typical murmur is an early diastolic decrescendo murmur, because the abnormal backward flow occurs while the aortic valve should be closed.

Part IV — Mitral Regurgitation (MR)

MR is systolic backward flow from LV to LA: LV systole → LA volume overload → LA enlargement; regurgitant volume returns to LV in diastole → LV volume overload/dilation. Patients may have exertional dyspnea, fatigue, palpitations, orthopnea, or other HF symptoms. LA enlargement increases AF risk.

The classic murmur is holosystolic, best heard at the apex, radiating to the axilla. Acute severe MR is different from chronic MR: the LA has no time to adapt, so LA and pulmonary venous pressures can rise abruptly. Recent MI plus sudden dyspnea, pulmonary edema, hypoxemia, and a new apical systolic murmur should raise concern for acute MR from papillary muscle dysfunction or rupture and requires emergency evaluation.

Part V — Mitral Stenosis (MS)

MS obstructs diastolic LA-to-LV flow: LA pressure ↑ → LA enlargement → pulmonary venous pressure ↑ → dyspnea. Chronic elevation can lead to pulmonary vascular change, pulmonary hypertension, increased RV afterload, and eventually right-sided HF. The typical murmur is a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex.

MS also provides an important integration chain: MS → LA enlargement → AF → stasis → atrial thrombus → embolic stroke. Tachycardia shortens diastole, leaving less time for flow across a narrowed mitral valve; LA pressure and pulmonary congestion can rise quickly, especially with rapid AF.

Part VI — Differential: Murmur plus Symptoms

Do not label every systolic murmur as AS. Use timing → location → radiation → quality/intensity → symptoms → patient context. AS is often RUSB to carotids; MR is apex to axilla; tricuspid regurgitation is often lower left sternal border; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and high-output flow murmurs are additional considerations. AS and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can both cause systolic ejection murmurs, but AS is a fixed outflow obstruction whereas HCM is dynamic; advanced assessment will cover maneuvers in detail.

With dyspnea plus a murmur, valve disease is only one possibility. Keep HF, CAD/ischemia, arrhythmia, pulmonary disease, anemia, pulmonary embolism when appropriate, and thyroid disease in the differential. Ask whether the murmur plausibly explains the presentation.

Part VII — Diagnostics

A murmur is a clue; transthoracic echocardiography defines structural and hemodynamic disease. It evaluates valve anatomy, stenosis/regurgitation severity, gradients/valve area when relevant, LV size and EF, LA size, pulmonary pressure estimates, and other structural disease. ECG can evaluate rhythm, LVH, conduction abnormalities, or prior ischemic changes. Chest imaging can help evaluate congestion, cardiomegaly, and pulmonary alternatives in dyspnea/HF. CBC, CMP/renal function/electrolytes, BNP/NT-proBNP, or thyroid studies should be selected to answer a clinical question rather than ordered automatically for every patient.

Consider echo promptly for a new murmur with dyspnea, syncope/presyncope, exertional chest symptoms, reduced exercise tolerance, HF findings, changing symptoms in known valve disease, unexplained pulmonary hypertension, or evidence of ventricular dysfunction. A symptomatic suspected structural lesion should not simply be observed indefinitely in primary care.

Part VIII — FNP Management, Referral, and Urgency

Medication often manages congestion, blood pressure, arrhythmia, HF, CAD, or thromboembolic risk; it does not usually correct a severe structural valve lesion. The FNP role is to identify disease, assess stability and severity, manage appropriate comorbidities, arrange surveillance, and refer appropriately. Anticoagulation in AF depends on the specific valve lesion, AF type, stroke risk, and current guideline context; do not assume one strategy fits every patient.

  • Routine outpatient characterization: incidental murmur, asymptomatic patient, and hemodynamic stability.
  • Expedited cardiology evaluation: suspected/known significant valve disease with new exertional dyspnea, declining tolerance, exertional chest symptoms, syncope/presyncope, or HF findings.
  • Emergency evaluation: severe respiratory distress, acute pulmonary edema, hypotension/shock, ongoing concerning chest pain, unstable syncope, suspected acute severe valve dysfunction, or post-MI new murmur with instability.

Part IX — Clinical Reasoning Cases

Case 1: A 78-year-old with progressive exertional dyspnea and lightheadedness has a harsh RUSB systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to both carotids. The likely diagnosis is AS, but the FNP-level next step is to assess structural severity with echocardiography and arrange timely cardiovascular evaluation.

Case 2: A 68-year-old with recent MI develops sudden severe dyspnea, hypoxemia, diffuse crackles, tachycardia, and a new apical systolic murmur. Think acute MR: papillary muscle dysfunction/rupture → sudden LV-to-LA regurgitation → LA pressure ↑↑ → pulmonary edema. This is an emergency.

Case 3: A 57-year-old with progressive dyspnea, palpitations, an irregularly irregular rhythm, apical diastolic murmur, and enlarged LA has a concerning MS–AF–stroke pathway. Integrate valve disease, AF, stasis, and thromboembolic risk rather than stopping at the murmur label.

FNP High-Yield Framework

  1. Timing: systolic or diastolic?
  2. Location and radiation: carotids, axilla, or elsewhere?
  3. Symptoms: dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, palpitations, edema?
  4. Hemodynamics: pressure overload or volume overload?
  5. Complications: HF, AF, pulmonary hypertension, stroke?
  6. Diagnostics: does this require echo now?
  7. Disposition: routine follow-up, cardiology, or emergency evaluation?

High-Yield Summary

  • AS: systolic RUSB → carotids; pressure overload/LVH; syncope, angina, dyspnea.
  • AR: early diastolic decrescendo; LV volume overload/dilation; possible wide pulse pressure.
  • MR: holosystolic apex → axilla; LA/LV volume overload; HF and AF risk; acute MR can cause pulmonary edema.
  • MS: diastolic apical rumble; LA enlargement, pulmonary congestion, AF and embolic stroke risk.
  • Symptoms plus a significant murmur require structural evaluation; hemodynamic instability requires emergency escalation.
